acl_id.description:
The ID to use for the acl, which will become the final component of the acl's name. The structure of 'aclId' defines the Resource Pattern (resource_type, resource_name, pattern_type) of the acl. 'aclId' is structured like one of the following:
For acls on the cluster: 'cluster'
For acls on a single resource within the cluster: 'topic/{resource_name}' 'consumerGroup/{resource_name}' 'transactionalId/{resource_name}'
For acls on all resources that match a prefix: 'topicPrefixed/{resource_name}' 'consumerGroupPrefixed/{resource_name}' 'transactionalIdPrefixed/{resource_name}'
For acls on all resources of a given type (i.e. the wildcard literal '*''): 'allTopics' (represents 'topic/*') 'allConsumerGroups' (represents 'consumerGroup/*') 'allTransactionalIds' (represents 'transactionalId/*').
acl_id.rationale: Identifier/name of the ACL resource (encoding the target resource pattern). It is a naming identifier rather than the access decision itself; the actual security controls are the principal, operation and permission_type entries. We do not constrain resource identifiers/names.

cluster.rationale: This is a reference to the cluster and does not impact access control itself.

deletion_policy.description:
Whether Terraform will be prevented from destroying the instance. Defaults to "DELETE".
When a 'terraform destroy' or 'terraform apply' would delete the instance,
the command will fail if this field is set to "PREVENT" in Terraform state.
When set to "ABANDON", the command will remove the resource from Terraform
management without updating or deleting the resource in the API.
When set to "DELETE", deleting the resource is allowed.

location.description: ID of the location of the Kafka resource. See https://cloud.google.com/managed-kafka/docs/locations for a list of supported locations.
location.rationale: Determines the region/zone where the resource is created. Policy should restrict it to an approved-region whitelist for data residency; the allowed set is parameterised (a hardcoded example whitelist is acceptable).

project.description: The ID of the project in which the resource belongs. If it is not provided, the provider project is used.
project.rationale: Project identifier used for resource scoping; does not define security posture of the resource.

acl_entries.description: The acl entries that apply to the resource pattern. The maximum number of allowed entries is 100.

acl_entries.host.description: The host. Must be set to "*" for Managed Service for Apache Kafka.
acl_entries.host.rationale: This is fixed for Managed Kafka and does not alter access scope beyond the ACL definition.

acl_entries.operation.description:
The operation type. Allowed values are (case insensitive): ALL, READ,
WRITE, CREATE, DELETE, ALTER, DESCRIBE, CLUSTER_ACTION, DESCRIBE_CONFIGS,
ALTER_CONFIGS, and IDEMPOTENT_WRITE. See https://kafka.apache.org/documentation/#operations_resources_and_protocols
for valid combinations of resource_type and operation for different Kafka API requests.
acl_entries.operation.rationale: Defining the operation type is vital for specifying what actions a principal can perform on Kafka resources. By restricting operations to only those necessary for a user's role, organizations can minimize the risk of accidental or malicious actions that could compromise data integrity or availability.

acl_entries.permission_type.description: The permission type. Accepted values are (case insensitive): ALLOW, DENY.
acl_entries.permission_type.rationale: Setting the permission type is essential for controlling access to Kafka resources. Using 'ALLOW' grants specific permissions to users, while 'DENY' can be used to explicitly restrict access. Properly configuring permission types helps enforce security policies and prevent unauthorized actions.

acl_entries.principal.description: The principal. Specified as Google Cloud account, with the Kafka StandardAuthorizer prefix User:". For example: "User:test-kafka-client@test-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com". Can be the wildcard "User:*" to refer to all users.
acl_entries.principal.rationale: Specifying the principal is crucial for defining who has access to Kafka resources. Using specific user accounts enhances security by limiting access to authorized individuals, while using wildcards can expose resources to unauthorized access.
